title: Diego Forlan Warns Uruguay: Be Careful Against India's Young Talent
excerpt: Ahead of Tuesday's historic India-Uruguay friendly in Kolkata, the 2010 World Cup Golden Ball winner says the Blue Tigers have "a lot of young footballing talent" — but need a stronger league and academies to develop them.
body:
• Uruguay head coach Diego Forlan warned his players to be "careful" against India ahead of the historic friendly at Kolkata's Salt Lake Stadium on Tuesday, saying India's players can "damage you" if given space.
  • Drawing on India's recent outing against Brazil, Forlan praised the Blue Tigers' young talent but said a stronger league and better academies are essential for developing them into regular competitors.
  • Forlan, who played for Mumbai City FC in the ISL in 2016, returns to India a decade later in a new role — as Uruguay's interim head coach, a job he calls "a great honour".
  • Uruguay arrive off a 4-1 win over South Korea but will be without key players including Federico Valverde, who is out injured.

Diego Forlan has played at Kolkata's Salt Lake Stadium before, kicked off exhibition matches there, and spent six months in Mumbai as Indian Super League royalty. On Tuesday, he walks out as the opposing manager — head coach of Uruguay — and he is refusing to treat India as a warm-up act. "Against Brazil, we saw that India have some good players," Forlan said at Monday's pre-match press conference. "You have to be careful against India. If we give them space, they can damage you."

Context & Background

The friendly caps a remarkable international window for Indian football — matches against Panama, Brazil and now Uruguay, two-time world champions, on home soil. Forlan, the 2010 World Cup Golden Ball winner with 112 Uruguay caps, took over as Uruguay's interim head coach after Marcelo Bielsa's departure, with a contract running to March 2027. He also leads Uruguay's under-20s. Uruguay reached Kolkata on September 30, a week ahead of the game, and the squad has been soaking in the city — visiting Eden Gardens to try cricket, touring the Victoria Memorial and St Paul's Cathedral. On the pitch this window they beat South Korea 4-1 away and lost 3-1 to Japan; Forlan felt the Japan defeat was undeserved. Key names are missing this time: Federico Valverde is out injured, Giorgian de Arrascaeta and Sebastián Cáceres returned home hurt, and Brian Rodríguez is unavailable.

Impact & Analysis

Forlan's assessment of Indian football is notable for its specificity. He did not offer the usual polite generalities. "Cricket is the main sport in India, but there is a lot of young footballing talent," he said. "Having a strong league would be important for developing these players. In the near future, India could be playing more competitive games." The diagnosis lands precisely where Indian football's debate sits: the country has the raw material, but converting talent into a competitive national side requires structural work — stronger leagues, better academies, more meaningful minutes. Forlan speaks from experience on this ground: he was Mumbai City FC's marquee signing in ISL 2016, scoring five goals in 12 matches, and first visited Kolkata back in July 2010 on a reality-show trip that drew thousands. Ten years on, he sees the same ingredients — "a really nice country with a lot of good footballers" — and is still waiting for the system around them to catch up.

"Cricket is the main sport in India, but there is a lot of young footballing talent. Having a strong league would be important for developing these players."

— Diego Forlan, Uruguay head coach

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora's football fans — from Premier League-watching families in London to the Indian-American youth soccer circuit — Forlan's verdict carries weight precisely because he knows the terrain. He has been inside Indian dressing rooms and Indian stadiums across three different decades. His message is the encouraging and frustrating kind: India is not short of footballers; it is short of pathways. For young Indian-origin players abroad choosing between cricket and football, a stronger Indian league would change the calculus of where a serious career can be built.

What's Next

Tuesday's friendly is a test India is set up to fail gracefully and learn from loudly — and India coach Khalid Jamil's squad knows it, coming off a 0-4 Saturday defeat and warning that "one mistake will cost us very badly" at this level. A competitive showing against a side that thrashed South Korea 4-1 would mean more than the result. For Forlan, the longer horizon is Uruguay's contract through March 2027 and the under-20 qualifiers in January — and, he smiles, the 2030 World Cup opener in Montevideo, 100 years after the first edition. India's horizon is simpler: turn a historic window of glamour friendlies into the competitive calendar Forlan says the country is almost ready for.
